more.title: Scientists find hidden materials that could improve batteries and solar fuels
more.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden world of “in-between” materials that briefly form as chemical ingredients are heated, revealing structures that conventional methods can miss. Among the discoveries is a previously unknown form of bismuth vanadate, a material widely studied for using sunlight to help produce clean hydrogen.

more.title: Geologists uncover evidence of a missing Late Cretaceous magmatic arc in northwestern Iran
more.summary: Mountains preserve evidence of ancient oceans, moving continents and tectonic processes that have shaped Earth over millions of years. Later deformation, erosion and burial, however, can obscure important parts of this geological record.

more.title: Bacteria turn a virus’ own weapon against it
more.summary: Researchers have uncovered a new way bacteria detect viral attacks: a virus-produced enzyme cuts a bacterial sensor protein, triggering a self-destructing immune response. The discovery could lead to more effective phage therapies against antibiotic-resistant bacteria and provide insight into ancient immune mechanisms shared with humans.

more.title: Food testing reveals how diet can add to exposure to 'forever chemicals'
more.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)—a vast family of chemicals used largely for their nonstick, water-repellent and grease-resistant properties—are called "forever chemicals" because of their remarkable resistance to degradation. They are now ubiquitous in our environment.

more.title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone
more.author: Jacek Krywko
more.summary: Dissolved rock precipitated around the tools, which then decayed.

more.title: Three quantum-inspired cores leave opposite fingerprints on the ringing of black holes
more.summary: Every black hole hides a question at its center. Einstein's theory predicts that whatever falls in is crushed into a singularity, a point of infinite density where the theory itself breaks down. Most physicists expect quantum gravity to replace that point with something finite. But the center lies hidden behind the horizon. How could we ever learn what is there?

more.title: What's been driving Hawaii's lava fountains?
more.author: John Timmer
more.summary: Before the lava fountains started, the ground was expanding by half a meter a day.

more.title: A 9-billion-year-old signal could help explain dark energy
more.summary: A Canadian radio telescope has detected the faint glow of hydrogen from billions of years ago using only its own observations, proving a long-awaited way to map the distant universe can actually work. CHIME can use this hydrogen signal to trace how matter is spread across space and measure how the universe has expanded over time, offering a powerful new way to investigate dark energy.

more.title: Adjustable nanosensors turn water pressure into fluorescent signals, with stiffness shaping sensitivity
more.summary: A novel nanovesicle-based platform developed at Institute of Science Tokyo can measure hydrostatic pressure by converting pressure-induced molecular changes into fluorescence signals.

more.title: Climate change drives new species combinations, prompting calls to rethink conservation goals
more.summary: The fact that ecosystems change is nothing new. What is new, however, is the speed and scale at which new species communities are emerging as a result of climate change. Processes that once unfolded over centuries or even millennia are now being observed within just a few decades.

more.title: Fluorescent imaging tracks metabolism of cells in real time
more.summary: Cornell researchers have designed a new, faster form of two-photon fluorescence imaging for observing cell metabolism in real time, a method that could enable quicker screening of new therapeutic treatments. The findings were published Sept. 4 in Science Advances. The co-lead authors are former postdoctoral researcher Lu Ling, Ph.D. '20, and doctoral student Jack Crowley, M.S. '22.

more.title: Polar oceans store carbon—but policy is not yet ready to count it
more.summary: Polar oceans may play an important role in storing carbon and supporting biodiversity, but current science and policy frameworks are not yet ready to fully recognize their potential.

more.title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Gamma’s Grant Lee, Engine’s Elia Wallen, and GV’s Crystal Huang on landing your first 1,000 customers
more.author: TechCrunch Events
more.summary: Leaders from Gamma, Engine, and Google Ventures join TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 to talk how to get your first customers. Register now to save up to $100. Grab a second pass at 50% off.

more.title: What a swordfish washing up on British Columbia's coast says about our changing oceans
more.summary: Filmmaker and outdoorsperson Quinn Barabash recently made headlines when he found a swordfish carcass nearly two meters (6.6 feet) long on the remote shores of Haida Gwaii in northern British Columbia.

more.title: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
more.author: Jennifer Ouellette
more.summary: New winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam for video of a roundworm and single-celled Dileptus.

more.title: Genetic analysis reveals that some specialty coffee seeds do not match their commercial identity
more.summary: Genetic analysis revealed that several seeds from a batch sold as Sidra were not, in fact, Sidra; their genetic profile was closer to that of Batian, a Kenyan variety.

more.title: Nightjar wings reveal a trade-off between hunting slowly and traveling far
more.summary: The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nocturnal migratory bird that travels between Europe and southern Africa each year. However, its wings are not only used for long-distance journeys. When hunting insects, the nightjar must be able to slow down, turn sharply and fly at low speeds. Researchers at Lund University have now shown how this trade-off is reflected in the bird's flight mechanics.

more.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: AI And Energy Top A Busy Lineup Of Large Rounds
more.author: Joanna Glasner
more.summary: As the AI startup boom progresses, investors appear to be leaving few niches unfunded. That was apparent in this week’s lineup of large funding rounds, which featured AI infrastructure providers, a foundational model developer, a content protection platform for the AI age, and other AI-focused startups among the top investment recipients.

more.title: Q&A: How does AI affect our engagement at work?
more.summary: AI is being integrated into our work at a growing rate. Andreas Bergqvist, a Ph.D. student at the Department of Information Technology, has teamed up with colleagues to investigate how AI, automation and robotization affect work engagement.

more.title: Are analytics making pro sports less fun? Fans and analysts remain divided
more.summary: Today, the discussions of sports analytics in the 2011 movie "Moneyball" often seem quaint. The idea of a team using data to find players who may be more valuable than meets the eye (and less expensive) no longer surprises anyone.

more.title: 'Mix-and-match' material's properties can be tuned by changing its metallic 'recipe'
more.summary: Scientists have created a new family of materials whose behavior can be tuned by changing their metallic "recipe"—opening new possibilities for uses including gas storage and sensing.
